_comment: Documented alternative conceptions for the rusting / conservation-of-mass topic, authored by the procedure in docs/misconception_library.md. Every persona for this topic is built on the first entry; the rest are recorded because the research was done. Ordering is by how well documented the conception is. Citations live in rust.sources.md. Note that rusting is usually studied alongside burning - students who say a burnt object must weigh less are running the same intuition - so several entries rest on combustion evidence, which is better documented than rusting itself.
canonical_explanation: The rusted nail weighs more, because the iron combines with oxygen from the air and that oxygen has mass.

misconceptions.name: Rust eats the nail away
misconceptions.belief: Rust is what happens when metal rots. It eats into the nail and slowly destroys it, and that is why old rusty stuff goes flaky and crumbles and eventually falls apart. Rust is not new stuff that arrived, it is the nail being eaten away. Every bit of rust you can see is a bit of nail that has gone.
misconceptions.predicts: The rusted nail weighs less, and the longer it is left out the lighter it gets, so a nail rusted right through would weigh hardly anything.
changes_only_when: you weigh the same nail yourself before and after on a balance good enough to show a change, and you have to read the number out loud
you have to say where the flaky stuff came from, if the nail was the only thing sitting there
you catch every scrap of the flaky stuff and weigh the nail and the flakes together
misconceptions.slides_into: That nothing was destroyed after all, the surface of the nail just changed into a different form, so nothing was lost and nothing added and it weighs the same as it always did.

misconceptions.name: The rust was in there all along
misconceptions.belief: The rust does not come from anywhere, it was already in the nail. It is what iron is like underneath, and being out in the wet just brings it out to the surface, like a stain coming through. Nothing gets added and nothing leaves. It is the same nail, just a different colour on the outside.
misconceptions.predicts: The rusted nail weighs exactly the same, because it is the identical nail and only its appearance changed. Wiping or scraping the rust off would give you back the nail you started with.
changes_only_when: you have to explain why a brand new nail straight out of the box has none of it anywhere on it
two identical nails are kept side by side, one sealed in a dry jar and one left out in the rain, and you have to say what was different about the two
you scrape all of it off and the nail underneath is visibly thinner than it started
misconceptions.slides_into: That the nail turned into a completely different substance, and a different substance just weighs whatever it weighs, so it could go either way.

misconceptions.name: Air does not weigh anything
misconceptions.belief: Air is nothing. It is just empty, you cannot hold it and you cannot feel it pressing down, so it cannot weigh anything. Even if something did join onto the nail while it sat out there, it would not make the nail any heavier, because there is nothing there to be heavy. Only solid stuff you can pick up has weight.
misconceptions.predicts: The rusted nail weighs the same. You can even name air as being involved and still say the weight did not change, because in your picture nothing weighable moved.
changes_only_when: a balloon pumped full is weighed against the same balloon empty, and you have to read both numbers
you see a sealed container weighed full and then weighed again after the gas is let out
you have to explain how a gas cylinder can be empty or full if the difference is nothing
misconceptions.slides_into: That air does weigh something but far less than solid stuff, so anything gassy involved must pull the total down rather than up.

misconceptions.name: A chemical reaction uses the stuff up
misconceptions.belief: When something reacts, the stuff gets used up. That is what a reaction is, the material gets spent, like petrol in a car or wood in a fire. There is less of it afterwards than there was before. The nail is reacting the whole time it sits out there, so there is less nail at the end.
misconceptions.predicts: The rusted nail weighs less, and being told a reaction is happening makes you more sure rather than less, because using things up is what reactions do.
changes_only_when: you weigh a closed jar with everything in it before and after, and the number does not do what you said it would
you have to say what the used-up part turned into, and where that went
somebody makes you separate there being less of the thing you can see from there being less stuff altogether
misconceptions.slides_into: That it is all still there but spread out, or turned into heat, or gone off as a gas you cannot see.

misconceptions.name: Nothing was added, so nothing can have changed
misconceptions.belief: Weight does not appear out of nowhere and it does not vanish either. Nobody put anything on the nail and nothing dropped off it, it just sat there. So it has to weigh exactly what it weighed before. Same nail, same weight.
misconceptions.predicts: The rusted nail weighs the same, and you defend it with the rule rather than by looking at what is around the nail. The rule settles it.
changes_only_when: you have to say out loud what counts as everything, when the nail is sitting out in the open with nothing round it
the same experiment is run once with a lid on and once with the lid off and the two give different numbers
somebody asks you to point at the boundary of the thing you just said nothing entered
misconceptions.slides_into: That it depends on whether there is a lid on, so a sealed jar conserves weight and an open one does not, with the lid doing the work rather than what is actually going in or out.
